section_summary: This section is dominated by May–June 1941 newspaper editorials, letters, cartoons, and reports protesting continued American petroleum exports to Japan while Harold L. Ickes warned of tanker shortages, gasoline restrictions, and “gasless Sundays” in the eastern United States. The clippings debate whether the shortage reflected inadequate transportation, diversion of American tankers to Britain, government policy, or oil-industry interests, and they describe Japanese ships loading petroleum at American ports. The final pages contain July–August State Department correspondence concerning Japanese bunkering in Brazil, Japanese inquiries about Bolivian rubber, Governor Culbert L. Olson’s demand for a complete embargo, and aviation gasoline storage at Dairen.

subfiles.title: Japanese tanker departure and cargo (fragment)
subfiles.about: Reports the departure of a tanker carrying oil and aviation gasoline with Japanese naval personnel aboard.
subfiles.summary: The fragment states that two Japanese naval officers and thirteen navy men accompanied the merchant crew. The vessel reportedly departed with 62,000 barrels of oil and 18,000 barrels of aviation gasoline loaded at Associated Oil docks.

subfiles.title: Is It Necessary?
subfiles.about: Questions proposed American fuel restrictions while petroleum continues to be exported to Japan and Russia.
subfiles.summary: The editorial accepts gasless Sundays, daylight saving, and reduced lighting only if a genuine defense need exists. It demands stronger authority than Ickes’s assertion and argues that domestic rationing should await the cessation of petroleum exports to Japan and Russia.

subfiles.title: Sunday driving, oil conservation, and exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Considers restrictions on Sunday driving and challenges continued petroleum shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The editorial suggests that closing filling stations for part of the weekend might reduce unnecessary driving without preventing church attendance and recreation. It expresses apprehension about Ickes’s authority over the oil industry and asks why gasoline and fuel oil still leave West Coast ports for Japan if conservation is essential to national defense.

subfiles.title: Federal control of the oil industry
subfiles.about: Reviews oil-industry opposition to Ickes’s appointment and fears of permanent federal control.
subfiles.summary: Lawrence describes administrative confusion over petroleum and explains why officials selected Ickes, citing his experience with the NRA Oil Code. Quoting publisher Ray L. Dudley, he records industry fears that federal coordination could become permanent public control and recalls criticism of Ickes’s conduct during the Madison oil antitrust case.

subfiles.title: No Sense to Gas Price Jump, Rideless Weekends
subfiles.about: Argues that the United States has abundant oil and that transportation, rather than supply, is the real problem.
subfiles.summary: Edson rejects claims of a physical petroleum shortage, citing restricted production in major American oil fields. He surveys tankers, railroad tank cars, trucks, and pipelines as alternative means of supplying the Atlantic seaboard and calls for better organization and infrastructure.

subfiles.title: “Gas” for the Axis
subfiles.about: Demands an explanation for petroleum exports to Japan and Russia while Americans face fuel restrictions.
subfiles.summary: Buttles contrasts threatened gasoline and heating restrictions with tanker transfers and continuing exports to Japan and Russia. He accuses the government and oil companies of aiding Axis partners and insists that Americans should not sacrifice for appeasement or profit.

subfiles.title: Why the Tanker Diversion?
subfiles.about: Questions the diversion of fifty American tankers to British service and its effect on eastern petroleum supplies.
subfiles.summary: The editorial asks Ickes and the Maritime Commission to justify transferring American tankers to Britain when the eastern United States already faced a tight supply situation. It compares British tanker capacity with wartime needs and asks whether lend-lease was being used to protect British commercial interests at American expense.

subfiles.title: Why the Tanker Diversion? (duplicate partial clipping)
subfiles.about: Reproduces most of the editorial questioning the transfer of American tankers to Britain.
subfiles.summary: This partial duplicate repeats the argument that fifty diverted tankers could create serious shortages on the American eastern seaboard. It again calls for public disclosure of Britain’s tanker needs and the commercial purposes served by vessels under British control.

subfiles.title: Give the People the Facts
subfiles.about: Calls for a public explanation of domestic petroleum sacrifices alongside increased sales to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The editorial says Americans will accept gasless Sundays and cooler homes if the need is explained. It contrasts the Petroleum Institute’s warnings with W. S. Farish’s announcement of additional sales to Japan and argues that such exports assist Japan against China and Germany against Britain.

subfiles.title: For U.S. Fuel—For Japan
subfiles.about: Contrasts American gasless Sundays with unrestricted petroleum supplies for Japan.
subfiles.summary: The cartoon depicts domestic motorists facing restrictions while fuel flows toward Japan. Its caption argues visually that conservation was being imposed unequally.

subfiles.title: Doesn’t Mr. Public Realize an Emergency?
subfiles.about: Satirizes government demands for American gasoline restraint while exports continue to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The cartoon juxtaposes warnings of a July shortage and restrictions for essential supplies with a conspicuous flow of gasoline to Japan. It presents the American public as being blamed for an emergency created by contradictory policy.

subfiles.title: Plug That Leak, Harold: How About Some Priorities Here?
subfiles.about: Urges Ickes to stop petroleum exports to Japan before restricting American motorists.
subfiles.summary: The editorial condemns continued petroleum sales after earlier controls on scrap metal and other strategic materials. Citing a sharp increase in March exports, it argues that Japanese purchases support aggression in China and should be halted before Americans accept gasless Sundays.

subfiles.title: Give the People the Facts (continued or duplicate fragment)
subfiles.about: Repeats and extends the editorial argument that the public deserves an explanation of petroleum policy.
subfiles.summary: The fragment repeats the contrast between threatened domestic restrictions and approved sales to Japan. It adds that the shortage lay in transportation and had been aggravated by transferring fifty coastwise tankers to British service.

subfiles.title: The Customer Across the Pacific
subfiles.about: Shows Japan claiming exemption from proposed American gas and oil rationing.
subfiles.summary: The cartoon portrays an “honorable” Japanese customer receiving American oil while the United States considers rationing and gasless Sundays. Its irony attacks preferential treatment of Japanese purchasers.

subfiles.title: Mr. Ickes’ Oil Shortage
subfiles.about: Blames tanker transfers and exports to Japan for the threatened American oil shortage.
subfiles.summary: The writer criticizes an administration that warns its own citizens of shortages while Japan receives roughly 70,000 barrels daily. The letter predicts further tanker transfers to Britain and portrays American policy as surrendering domestic resources to foreign powers.

subfiles.title: Gas Rationing in Britain—Should Interest Mr. Ickes
subfiles.about: Uses Britain’s experience to warn that strict gasoline rationing could disrupt American defense production.
subfiles.summary: The editorial notes that Britain restored many private cars after discovering that workers could not efficiently reach factories without them. It argues that automobiles are even more integral to American life and that rigid rationing could impair rather than aid defense work.

subfiles.title: Appears to Be Writ Sarcastic
subfiles.about: Sarcastically requests a bicycle for visiting tankers loading petroleum for Japan at Richmond.
subfiles.summary: The writer asks where a bicycle can be rented for the impending gasless Sundays. The stated purpose is to ride to Richmond and watch tankers load gas and oil for Japan.

subfiles.title: Ickes Takes Control of Oil; Shipping to Be Major Problem
subfiles.about: Reports Roosevelt’s appointment of Ickes as petroleum coordinator and identifies transportation as the immediate supply problem.
subfiles.summary: Roosevelt directs Ickes to coordinate the American petroleum industry so military and civilian requirements can be met continuously and at reasonable prices. The report says crude supplies were adequate but diversion of tankers to aid Britain had created a distribution bottleneck, particularly on the Atlantic seaboard.

subfiles.title: Roll Out the Barrels—Softly
subfiles.about: Condemns secrecy surrounding large oil exports to Japan while Americans are warned to expect rationing.
subfiles.summary: The editorial calculates annualized exports from the March 1941 figure of 1,553,000 barrels and argues that Japan is accumulating oil for future war. It compares American export secrecy with prewar French trade with Germany and appeals directly to Roosevelt to end a policy that undermines public confidence in defense and lend-lease.

subfiles.title: The Case for Continuing Limited Oil Shipments to Japan
subfiles.about: Explains strategic arguments for continuing petroleum sales to Japan while reserving the option of cutting them if American needs require it.
subfiles.summary: The editorial acknowledges public anger but says an embargo might provoke demands to halt aid to China or push Japan toward the Dutch East Indies. It argues that limited supplies may help keep Japan out of the European war, although shipments could legitimately be reduced if American tankers or petroleum were required for defense.

subfiles.title: The Customer Across the Pacific (duplicate cartoon)
subfiles.about: Repeats the cartoon portraying Japan as exempt from American fuel rationing.
subfiles.summary: The cartoon again contrasts proposed gasless Sundays and oil rationing in the United States with continuing service to an “honorable” customer across the Pacific. Japan’s exemption is the object of the satire.

subfiles.title: Vulnerability
subfiles.about: Warns that German long-range aviation and possible Atlantic bases make the United States vulnerable to attack.
subfiles.summary: The editorial challenges the belief that oceans make the United States immune from invasion or bombing. Citing Aviation, it describes German bombers potentially operating against New York, Panama, and eastern aircraft factories from European, African, or Atlantic-island bases, and concludes that aid to Britain is essential.

subfiles.title: Are Ya Listenin’?
subfiles.about: Illustrates Göring’s claim that no island is unconquerable by naming vulnerable Atlantic and Caribbean islands.
subfiles.summary: The cartoon places the Azores, Bermuda, the Bahamas, Martinique, and Cape Verde beneath Göring’s declaration about islands. It reinforces contemporary fears that Axis expansion could reach bases near the Americas.

subfiles.title: He Must Find New Means to Deliver the Oil
subfiles.about: Profiles Ickes and outlines his responsibilities as Petroleum Coordinator for National Defense.
subfiles.summary: The profile recounts Ickes’s New Deal career, reputation, and contentious relationship with private industry. It emphasizes that the threatened shortage was chiefly a transportation problem caused by tanker diversions to Britain and describes proposed pipelines, new tankers, and more efficient use of existing facilities.

subfiles.title: Why Does the United States Go On Selling Oil to Japan?
subfiles.about: Questions the strategic logic and morality of continuing American petroleum exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The editorial says petroleum companies claim they will stop exports whenever the State Department directs them to do so. It presents the government’s fear that an embargo would drive Japan toward the Netherlands Indies but asks whether the United States should show less resolve than the Dutch colonial government.

subfiles.title: Gasless Sundays
subfiles.about: Opposes domestic gasoline restrictions while an Axis partner continues receiving American oil.
subfiles.summary: The writer supports unrestricted aid to Britain but rejects gasless Sundays that would free more petroleum for Japan. The letter urges Americans to protest and to stop supplies to Axis partners before accepting further sacrifices.

subfiles.title: More Facts on the Gasoline ‘Shortage’
subfiles.about: Uses British tanker statistics to question the diversion of American vessels and the resulting New England shortage.
subfiles.summary: The item quotes Wall Street Journal figures on Britain’s prewar and acquired tanker fleet. It suggests Britain retained more than enough vessels for its calculated wartime oil requirements and argues that New Englanders deserve a detailed government explanation.

subfiles.title: The Customer Across the Pacific
subfiles.about: Publishes the recurring cartoon contrasting American rationing with petroleum sales to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Tacoma Times reproduces the “honorable customer” cartoon on its front page. The image presents Japan as exempt from restrictions that might produce gasless Sundays for Americans.

subfiles.title: Japanese Ship Loads Oil Here as East Faces ‘Gasless Sundays’
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese freighters loading petroleum at Philadelphia and other eastern ports despite the tanker shortage.
subfiles.summary: The article describes the Azuma Maru and other Japanese freighters taking lubricating oil and gasoline from Philadelphia-area docks while eastern consumers face possible restrictions. It says three or four Japanese ships monthly carried petroleum from eastern ports and discusses legal exports below the aviation-gasoline embargo threshold. It also examines American-owned tankers shifted to Panamanian registry while noting the Maritime Commission’s denial that such tankers were hauling oil to Japan.

subfiles.title: It’s About Time
subfiles.about: Welcomes Ickes’s intervention against a lubricating-oil shipment from Philadelphia to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The editorial calls it incongruous to send 252,000 gallons of lubricating oil from the eastern seaboard while residents there face petroleum rationing. It urges rapid action against similar Atlantic shipments, questions continued Pacific Coast exports, and proposes building domestic oil reserves.

subfiles.title: Honest, Harold?
subfiles.about: Challenges Ickes’s call for domestic economy while large quantities of oil go to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The cartoon shows Ickes telling motorists and homeowners to economize because of a tanker shortage. Beside him, oil wells feed a stream labeled “800,000 barrels a month for the Japanese war machine.”

subfiles.title: Japanese War Machine Running on U.S. Gasoline
subfiles.about: Depicts Japan’s war machine passing an America halted by a gasless Sunday.
subfiles.summary: The cartoon shows a Japanese military vehicle fueled by American gasoline. The United States is simultaneously immobilized by a sign announcing “Gasless Sunday.”

subfiles.title: Gasoline Shortage Just Another Foolish Bugaboo
subfiles.about: Denies that the United States faces a genuine gasoline shortage and questions the motives behind the warning.
subfiles.summary: The writer argues that prorated American oil fields could rapidly flood the market if allowed to produce freely. The letter suggests the scare may serve higher prices or government control under Ickes and asks why gasoline continues to be shipped to Tokyo.

subfiles.title: Gasless Sundays
subfiles.about: Discusses the social cost of Sunday motoring restrictions and distrust of Ickes.
subfiles.summary: The editorial says Americans would accept necessary conservation but objects that Ickes is an unpopular and authoritarian messenger. It contrasts 1941 automobile dependence with 1918 and argues that Sunday travel provides essential recreation and morale for workers, especially those laboring on defense projects.

subfiles.title: Gasless Sunday
subfiles.about: Proposes weekday automobile pooling as a less disruptive alternative to banning Sunday pleasure driving.
subfiles.summary: The editorial explains that automobiles had become necessities and that Sunday was the principal opportunity for family recreation. Accepting that eastern transportation shortages might require conservation, it suggests neighborhood weekday car pools rather than eliminating the family holiday.

subfiles.title: Japanese War Machine Running on U.S. Gasoline (duplicate cartoon)
subfiles.about: Repeats the cartoon contrasting Japanese use of American gasoline with a gasless Sunday at home.
subfiles.summary: The duplicate shows Japan’s war machine proceeding on U.S. gasoline while America is stopped. An Interior Department receipt stamp records its arrival on June 18, 1941.

subfiles.title: A Visitor from Japan: Japanese Vessel Here to Load Oil
subfiles.about: Reports that the Azuma Maru would load 1,500 barrels of lubricating oil in Philadelphia under a government license.
subfiles.summary: The report says the oil was apparently destined for Japan’s air force in China and quotes Laurence M. Hunter confirming that the cargo was licensed. It compares the shipment with threatened eastern fuel curtailment and estimates both monthly Japanese loadings at Philadelphia and the local impact of tanker diversions.

subfiles.title: Japanese Vessel Here to Load Oil (duplicate clipping)
subfiles.about: Duplicates the report on the Azuma Maru’s licensed loading of lubricating oil.
subfiles.summary: This second copy again states that the Japanese freighter would take on 1,500 barrels at Pier 98 before proceeding through New York to Japan. It repeats estimates of Philadelphia petroleum consumption, Japanese monthly exports, and the reduction in deliveries caused by government use of tankers.

subfiles.title: 800,000 Barrels of Oil a Month Going to Japan
subfiles.from: Joseph Driscoll, New York Herald Tribune
subfiles.about: Investigates the scale of American oil shipments to Japan and the administration’s hesitation to impose an embargo.
subfiles.summary: Driscoll reports that more than 800,000 barrels a month were going to Japan while New York, New England, and the eastern seaboard faced gasless Sundays. He argues that an embargo could release tankers for Atlantic supply and aid to Britain, but says the State Department feared provoking Japan toward the Dutch East Indies or endangering aid to China. William P. Cole Jr. is quoted urging correction if Japanese shipments materially contributed to the tanker shortage.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Japanese bunkering in the American republics
subfiles.about: Recommends an urgent response to Rio concerning petroleum sales to Japanese vessels.
subfiles.summary: Bonsal argues that prospective shortages make it undesirable to distribute petroleum in ways that do not support inter-American commerce or defense. He links the Rio telegram to the broader question of bunkering Japanese vessels already under departmental consideration.

subfiles.title: Telegram 1026 concerning Japanese purchases at Brazilian ports
subfiles.about: Reports excessive Japanese purchases of petroleum products and lubricants in Brazilian ports.
subfiles.summary: Standard Oil advises the embassy that Japanese vessels are buying petroleum products far beyond shipboard needs. The company asks whether it should refuse all supply or merely sales exceeding normal requirements.

subfiles.title: Instructions on petroleum sales to Japanese vessels in Brazil
subfiles.about: Directs American oil companies in Brazil to restrict Japanese purchases to necessary shipboard supplies.
subfiles.summary: Hull recommends limiting sales to estimated shipboard needs and requesting payment in dollars. The embassy may tell Brazil that Japanese overstocking is viewed unfavorably and could affect tanker allocations, pending establishment of a definitive American bunkering policy.

subfiles.title: Telegram 1025 on possible Brazilian requisition of oil
subfiles.about: Reports that the Brazilian Navy is examining whether to requisition the oil in question.
subfiles.summary: Caffery sends a brief update from Rio de Janeiro. He states that the Brazilian Navy is considering requisitioning the petroleum involved in the related case.

subfiles.title: British Embassy letter on Japanese inquiries about Bolivian rubber
subfiles.about: Warns that Japanese representatives are seeking samples and information about Bolivian Yungas rubber.
subfiles.summary: The letter identifies the Yungas as the forested rubber-producing region east of La Paz and describes the traditional export route through Pará with Amazon production. Although quantities were expected to be modest, the writer suspects Japan may seek a route avoiding Brazilian export restrictions and suggests addressing this in negotiations with Bolivia.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of British report on Bolivian rubber
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the warning about Japanese interest in Bolivian rubber and reports a request for investigation.
subfiles.summary: Finletter thanks the British correspondent for the July 18 letter. He states that the Department has instructed the American Legation at La Paz to investigate the matter.

subfiles.title: White House memorandum concerning Governor Olson’s telegram
subfiles.about: Requests that the State Department acknowledge Governor Olson’s telegram.
subfiles.summary: The brief memorandum forwards Olson’s communication to the State Department. It asks the Under Secretary to arrange an acknowledgment on behalf of the President.

subfiles.title: Governor Olson’s telegram urging a complete embargo on Japan
subfiles.from: Culbert L. Olson, Governor of California
subfiles.about: Calls for an immediate, complete embargo on oil, petroleum products, and other war materials destined for Japan.
subfiles.summary: Olson says Californians oppose supplying materials used for Japanese aggression and Axis plans, particularly after Japan’s advances in Indochina and toward the Dutch East Indies. He urges that the Tatsuta Maru, then in San Francisco Harbor with silk, be denied oil, gasoline, or other war cargo for its return voyage.

subfiles.title: Reply to Governor Olson on petroleum-export controls
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Olson’s embargo appeal and refers him to federal measures announced on August 1.
subfiles.summary: Hull conveys the President’s appreciation for Olson’s telegram and welcomes the indication of Californian opinion. He states that press accounts had described the government’s August 1 measures regarding petroleum exports.

subfiles.title: Telegram on aviation gasoline stored at Dairen
subfiles.about: Reports the delivery of Japanese aviation gasoline to leased Standard Oil storage tanks at Dairen.
subfiles.summary: Chase reports that a third tank leased from Standard Oil was partly filled with aviation gasoline discharged by a small tanker from Japan. Several voyages would be required to fill it, and additional gasoline in drums had also recently arrived. Copies were transmitted or mailed to American posts in Tokyo, Beijing, Shenyang, Harbin, Chongqing, and Shanghai.
